stories.headline: File updated compliance on flood-control measures, water bodies’ protection: HC to Govt
stories.title: File updated compliance on flood-control measures, water bodies’ protection: HC to Govt
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 26: The High Court of J&K and Ladakh has sought updated instructions in keeping with its order of May 29, 2024 regarding implementation of flood management, removal of encroachments and protection of water bodies across Kashmir, even as the utilisation certificates of Rs 413.23 crore funds released by the Union of India towards various flood protection projects. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal sought to update the instructions while hearing Environmental Policy Group’s (EPG) Public Interest Litigation (PIL), seeking measures to avoid devastation caused by a flood like 2014 in Kashmir. Following the 2014 floods, a batch of PILs which included EPG, had projected government’s indolence over flood management and lack of policy to deal with floods in Kashmir. These PILs highlighted the need for indispensable restoration of water bodies including Jehlum to their original width by doing away with the encroachments. In its May 29, 2024 order, the High Court pointed out that its orders were not being implemented properly and pulled up the authorities for being dilatory towards court directions. The court had issued a series of directions taking note of the need to prevent a recurrence of the devastating September 2014 floods and ensure the protection and restoration of the River Jhelum and other water bodies. It had directed the authorities to file a detailed affidavit explaining the steps taken in compliance with its earlier orders. The court had observed that the status report submitted by Union of India on January 13, 2022 indicated that funds of Rs 413.23 crore were released by the Centre towards various flood-management projects which included river Jhelum its tributaries and various Nallahs in different districts besides flood spill channels. The government was directed to furnish utilisation certificates for these funds released by the Centre. Furthermore, the court had further sought an updated compliance report regarding the prohibition on construction near water bodies and details, in tabulated form, of encroachments removed along the River Jhelum. It had also directed the government to submit an Action Taken Report detailing the preventive measures undertaken and envisaged to address the recurring threat of floods in Kashmir, besides filing an affidavit on steps taken towards demarcation of protected areas as directed in the court's August 18, 2017 order. The EPG’s PIL, along with connected matters relate to flood prevention, restoration of the River Jhelum and its tributaries, removal of encroachments and preservation of wetlands, lakes, forests and other ecologically sensitive areas.

stories.headline: Infra push, anti-doping steps highlighted by India in meet with IOC Future Host panel
stories.title: Infra push, anti-doping steps highlighted by India in meet with IOC Future Host panel
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 26: Highlighting the rapid development of sports infrastructure in the country and "aggressive anti-doping measures" in the last couple of years, India presented its roadmap for hosting the 2036 Olympic and Paralympic Games in an online interaction with the International Olympic Committee's Future Host Commission here on Thursday. The 30-minute presentation on Ahmedabad's preparedness was spearheaded by outgoing Indian Olympic Association President P T Usha and its CEO Raghuram Iyer. This was followed by a brief discussion with the Kolinda Grabar-Kitarovic-led nine-member Future Host Commission. According to a reliable source, the exchange after the presentation lasted about 20 minutes during which the Commission members posed queries related to India's planned budget, the measures that would be taken to ensure sustainability of venues, issues related to "clean sports", athlete experience and how the Games would help the Olympic movement in the country. "The entire Commission joined the online presentation from various parts of the world. The exchange was positive. Apart from highlighting the infrastructure push, we also spoke about the tough anti-doping measures being taken to curb the use of prohibited substances," the source told PTI. "The Commission was keen to know about the sustainability measures that will be taken to ensure that the venues don't lie dormant after the Games. They were satisfied with the way India responded and the general sentiment towards our vision was positive," the source added. India has significantly scaled up testing and is also working towards criminalising doping through legislation that would introduce jail terms and hefty fines on those involved in supplying banned substances to athletes. Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, who attended Thursday's meet at the Sports Authority of India headquarters here, has asserted repeatedly that doping would be addressed at a war footing. India has been topping the World Anti-Doping Agency's list of most violators among major nations for the last three years. In a press release issued after the meeting, the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) said the presentation covered proposed host city Ahmedabad's preparedness. "It also covered India's experience in hosting major international sporting events, proposed venue development plans, and the long-term vision for delivering the Games," stated the IOA. "I mean it's still very early days. There is a long way to go and lots of preparations to be done," said IOA CEO Raghuram Iyer after the meeting, referring to the three stages of dialogue that will follow the current Continuous Dialogue phase of the bidding process.

stories.headline: Antibiotic resistance threat grows in Kashmir
stories.title: Antibiotic resistance threat grows in Kashmir
stories.summary: Expert calls for tighter curbs on sale of high-end antibiotics outside hospitals Uniform antibiotic policy urged across healthcare institutions ‘Most winter infections are viral, don’t require antibiotics’ Srinagar, Nov 26: Rampant misuse, self-medication and indiscriminate prescriptions are fuelling antibiotic resistance in Kashmir, raising concerns that life-saving drugs could become ineffective against common infections. Experts have called for urgent regulatory measures and responsible antibiotic use to tackle the growing threat. Every year, World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week (WAAW) is observed from November 18 to 24 to raise awareness about antimicrobial resistance (AMR), with concerns mounting over easy over-the-counter access to antibiotics and gaps in prescription enforcement. Dr Syed Mudasir Qadri, Additional Professor, Department of Internal and Pulmonary Medicine, SKIMS, described the ever-increasing antimicrobial resistance as a ‘silent pandemic’ that requires urgent attention. “It is going on unabated, and if corrective measures are not taken well in time, we may end up with no antibiotics to treat us and our future generations,” he said. Qadri said people need to understand that not every infection requires systemic antibiotics, including oral, intravenous or intramuscular drugs, particularly when the infection is not caused by bacteria. He said the ongoing transition from autumn to winter, marked by falling temperatures and dry air, makes people more vulnerable to viral infections, many of which do not require antibiotic treatment. “The majority of these infections don't need antibiotic therapy, but people start self-medicating by taking over-the-counter antibiotics on their own,” he said. Qadri also expressed concern over the prescription of multiple or high-end antibiotics for simple infections that could be treated with first-line oral drugs. “There is a strong need to implement strict drug regulations on the availability of antibiotics, especially high-end parenteral antibiotics outside hospitals. Inside hospitals, we need to have permanently running Antimicrobial Stewardship Programmes (AMSP),” he said. Antimicrobial Stewardship is a structured programme aimed at combating AMR through the rational use of antibiotics. Qadri said the programme has been successfully running at SKIMS for the past eight years. Qadri said a uniform antibiotic policy is central to the programme and should initially be implemented across all PHCs, CHCs, district hospitals, GMCs and other healthcare institutions. At a later stage, he said, these measures could also be extended to the private healthcare sector. “A uniform antibiotic policy is like a guideline that all doctors follow for the treatment of infections, whether it is empirical therapy, definitive therapy or even prophylactic therapy,” he said. Qadri said such a policy could significantly help reduce antibiotic resistance and improve culture positivity rates, as observed at SKIMS following the implementation of its Antimicrobial Stewardship Programme. He also stressed the importance of preventing infections to reduce antibiotic consumption. “The other important step to reduce antibiotic consumption is prevention of infections. This can be achieved by following the usual principles of cleanliness, eating healthy food, keeping yourself warm in winters, following your doctor's advice and, of course, vaccination whenever and wherever prescribed by your doctor,” he said. Highlighting the challenges in developing new antibiotics, Qadri said the first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered accidentally by Alexander Fleming in 1928. He said no new class of antibiotics has been introduced into the market since 1987, a period often referred to as the 'discovery void'. “Developing a new antibiotic is a huge task even in this era of huge technological advancement. It takes years and sometimes decades to get a new antibiotic into the market for human use. On top of this, rampant and inappropriate use of antibiotics has led to the emergence of resistance to a wide variety of antibiotics, rendering them useless for treating infections,” he said. Doctors warn that the growing use of antibiotics also exposes patients to adverse effects and places an additional financial burden on individuals, hospitals and the public healthcare system due to the high cost of treatment. Qadri said antibiotics should be avoided for viral illnesses such as the common cold and flu, which are prevalent during the winter season. “Majority of infections are viral in origin and do not require antibiotics. People need to be aware and responsible and not fall into the trap of using antibiotics when just paracetamol or other symptomatic treatment may be enough,” he said. He said the irrational use of antibiotics was a serious public health concern requiring stronger policy interventions and effective enforcement at the national level. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), in a report last year, also warned that antibiotics were increasingly proving ineffective against common infections such as pneumonia and urinary tract infections (UTIs), largely due to their indiscriminate and irrational use, highlighting the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance.

stories.title: Bihar move illegal, says Supreme Court, quashes premature release of former MP
stories.summary: In a significant ruling, the Supreme Court has annulled the Bihar government's controversial decision to release Anand Mohan, who was serving time for murder. The state's attempt to modify prison regulations for his early exit was found unconstitutional. Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu criticized the justification threshold for such a change, ultimately mandating that Anand Mohan must surrender within a month.

These sanctions involve officials implicated in collusion with builders in housing fraud schemes. The banks' CMDs must articulate their non-compliance in court if not met within a week. CBI’s investigations have led to chargesheets, and trials will commence once the necessary sanctions are secured, underscoring the urgency for timely judicial processes.

stories.headline: Central University of Kashmir celebrates Constitution Day
stories.title: Central University of Kashmir celebrates Constitution Day
stories.summary: Ganderbal, Nov 26: The Department of Law, School of Legal Studies (SLS), Central University of Kashmir (CUK), celebrated Constitution Day-2026 under the theme “Hamara Samvidhan-Hamara Swabhiman” at the Tulmulla campus here on Thursday. The programme commemorated the adoption of the Constitution of India and reaffirmed the University's commitment to constitutional values and the principles enshrined in the founding document. In his keynote address (online), former Judge of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Hon'ble Justice Paramjit Singh Dhaliwal, deliberated extensively on the concept of constitutionalism and the evolution of the basic structure doctrine, describing them as essential safeguards for preserving the constitutional framework. Drawing upon his extensive experience in the legal profession, he shared insights into the relationship between the Constitution, the legislature, the executive and the judiciary. He observed that constitutionalism was reflected not merely in judicial pronouncements but also in the conduct of citizens and public institutions, particularly in their commitment to upholding the rule of law. He elaborated on the historical evolution of the relationship between Parliament and the judiciary concerning the power to amend the Constitution, tracing important judicial developments from the early constitutional cases to the landmark Kesavananda Bharati judgment of 1973. Justice Dhaliwal also reflected upon the warnings articulated by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar in his concluding address to the Constituent Assembly, particularly against unconstitutional methods in politics and the absence of social democracy. He urged law students to develop independent thinking, engage critically with constitutional questions and support their arguments with reason and sound legal understanding. He emphasised that the true strength of constitutional democracy depended not only upon the institutions established under the Constitution but also upon the integrity, awareness and conduct of those who served and upheld it. Earlier, in his welcome address, Dean, School of Legal Studies, Prof. Farooq Ahmad Mir, emphasised that Constitution Day was not merely a ceremonial occasion but an opportunity to reflect upon the responsibilities that the Constitution places upon every citizen. Highlighting the significance of engaging students in the process of social transformation, he observed that meaningful change in society could be achieved only when students, teachers and families collectively became instruments of positive change. Referring to the Preamble, he underscored that the Constitution belongs to every citizen, irrespective of caste, creed, religion, region or language. He highlighted its commitment to securing social, economic and political justice, liberty of thought and expression, equality of status and opportunity, and fraternity, assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation. Tracing the making of the Constitution, Prof. Mir observed that it was the outcome of immense intellectual effort, deliberations and the sacrifices associated with India's freedom struggle. He noted that the Constituent Assembly took two years, eleven months and eighteen days to complete the historic task, with its members engaging in extensive discussions and deliberations before giving the country its Constitution. He further observed that the Constitution was a dynamic document whose relevance continued to be strengthened through judicial interpretation in response to the changing needs of society. The programme proceedings were conducted by Assistant Professor Dr. Gulafroz Jan, who also read the Preamble to the Constitution, with participants reaffirming their commitment to its ideals. Associate Professor Dr. Jehirul Islam proposed the vote of thanks. The Constitution Day Preamble reading and pledge-taking exercise were also organised across all campuses of the University. Meanwhile, the Directorate of Students Welfare also organised a debate competition as part of the Constitution Day celebrations.

body: In his keynote address (online), former Judge of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Hon'ble Justice Paramjit Singh Dhaliwal, deliberated extensively on the concept of constitutionalism and the evolution of the basic structure doctrine, describing them as essential safeguards for preserving the constitutional framework.
Drawing upon his extensive experience in the legal profession, he shared insights into the relationship between the Constitution, the legislature, the executive and the judiciary.

He observed that constitutionalism was reflected not merely in judicial pronouncements but also in the conduct of citizens and public institutions, particularly in their commitment to upholding the rule of law.

He elaborated on the historical evolution of the relationship between Parliament and the judiciary concerning the power to amend the Constitution, tracing important judicial developments from the early constitutional cases to the landmark Kesavananda Bharati judgment of 1973.

Justice Dhaliwal also reflected upon the warnings articulated by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar in his concluding address to the Constituent Assembly, particularly against unconstitutional methods in politics and the absence of social democracy.
He urged law students to develop independent thinking, engage critically with constitutional questions and support their arguments with reason and sound legal understanding.

He emphasised that the true strength of constitutional democracy depended not only upon the institutions established under the Constitution but also upon the integrity, awareness and conduct of those who served and upheld it.

Earlier, in his welcome address, Dean, School of Legal Studies, Prof. Farooq Ahmad Mir, emphasised that Constitution Day was not merely a ceremonial occasion but an opportunity to reflect upon the responsibilities that the Constitution places upon every citizen.

Highlighting the significance of engaging students in the process of social transformation, he observed that meaningful change in society could be achieved only when students, teachers and families collectively became instruments of positive change.
Referring to the Preamble, he underscored that the Constitution belongs to every citizen, irrespective of caste, creed, religion, region or language.

He highlighted its commitment to securing social, economic and political justice, liberty of thought and expression, equality of status and opportunity, and fraternity, assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation.
Tracing the making of the Constitution, Prof. Mir observed that it was the outcome of immense intellectual effort, deliberations and the sacrifices associated with India's freedom struggle.

He noted that the Constituent Assembly took two years, eleven months and eighteen days to complete the historic task, with its members engaging in extensive discussions and deliberations before giving the country its Constitution.
He further observed that the Constitution was a dynamic document whose relevance continued to be strengthened through judicial interpretation in response to the changing needs of society.
The programme proceedings were conducted by Assistant Professor Dr. Gulafroz Jan, who also read the Preamble to the Constitution, with participants reaffirming their commitment to its ideals.
Associate Professor Dr. Jehirul Islam proposed the vote of thanks.
The Constitution Day Preamble reading and pledge-taking exercise were also organised across all campuses of the University.
Meanwhile, the Directorate of Students Welfare also organised a debate competition as part of the Constitution Day celebrations.

stories.headline: No content from Pakistan to be shown in India, government reminds Netflix
stories.title: No content from Pakistan to be shown in India, government reminds Netflix
stories.summary: In a move reflecting ongoing tensions, the Indian Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has urged Netflix to limit access to Pakistani content, particularly an upcoming series set to debut on December 4. This action follows previous advisories related to national security concerns amid the India-Pakistan conflict. Netflix has not clarified the series' availability in India, as industry groups pursue legal actions against Pakistani media.

stories.title: Centre sanctions Rs 50L for model Sub-Registrar office
stories.summary: Vijayawada MP Kesineni Sivanath announces Rs 50 lakh first-phase sanction for a PSK-model Sub-Registrar office under DILRMP 3.0 and NAKSHA schemes.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Vijayawada MP Kesineni Sivanath announces Rs 50 lakh first-phase sanction for a PSK-model Sub-Registrar office under DILRMP 3.0 and NAKSHA schemes.

The Centre has sanctioned Rs.50 lakh in the first phase for setting up a state-of-the-art model Sub-Registrar office in Vijayawada on the lines of a Passport Seva Kendra (PSK), Vijayawada MP Kesineni Sivanath (Chinni) announced on Thursday.
Welcoming the decision, the MP said the Centre had responded positively to his repeated representations to Union Ministers seeking improved property registration facilities for people in Vijayawada.

The proposed model office will be established under the Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme (DILRMP) 3.0 and NAKSHA schemes, aimed at modernising land records and improving registration-related services.

stories.headline: Vikramaditya Singh seeks expert scrutiny over construction near Sheshnag
stories.title: Vikramaditya Singh seeks expert scrutiny over construction near Sheshnag
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 26: Former MLC of Congress, Vikramaditya Singh, has raised concerns over Border Roads Organisation (BRO) construction near Sheshnag Lake, warning that unchecked activity could cause irreversible damage to the fragile glacial ecosystem. Vikramaditya is grandson of Maharaja Hari Singh, the last Dogra ruler of Jammu and Kashmir, and son of former Sadr-e-Riyasat Dr Karan Singh. “The felling and burning of protected Chinar and Chestnut trees in Kashmir, along with BRO road construction in close proximity to the sacred Sheshnag Lake, are deeply concerning developments,” he said. “The experiences of Uttarakhand and Nepal serve as stark reminders of the consequences of unchecked / over-development and environmental neglect. The fragile ecosystem of Jammu & Kashmir, already under considerable stress, cannot afford such irreversible damage.” “It is our collective duty to preserve the natural beauty and unique ecology of Jammu & Kashmir for future generations.” “I urge the J&K Government and the concerned authorities to take serious cognisance of these activities and ensure strict monitoring before it is too late,” Singh wrote on X. He was responding to a post by environmental activist and Jammu and Kashmir Climate Action Group chairman Dr Raja Muzaffar Bhat, who sought an expert assessment of excavation and track-widening near the lake. Bhat had asked glaciologist and Islamic University of Science and Technology (IUST) Vice-Chancellor Prof Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, J&K Pollution Control Committee chairman Vasu Yadav and Chief Wildlife Warden Sarvesh Rai to examine the works, particularly their potential impact on the lake, glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) risks and surrounding alpine habitats. Singh also called on Environment and Forest Minister Altaf Ahmad Kaloo to facilitate a joint briefing by the experts.

stories.headline: CM stresses time-bound execution of key projects in Ramban
stories.title: CM stresses time-bound execution of key projects in Ramban
stories.summary: Ramban, Nov 26: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Thursday called for expediting ongoing works, addressing gaps in service delivery and ensuring equitable development, particularly in remote and difficult-to-access areas. He was chairing a comprehensive review meeting of the developmental scenario in Ramban district, taking stock of progress on key infrastructure projects, delivery of essential public services and implementation of welfare schemes. During his visit, the Chief Minister inaugurated nine developmental works worth Rs 54.72 Cr and laid the foundation stone for another project worth Rs 3.26 Cr, taking the total investment to Rs 57.98 Cr. The major projects include upgradation of the Patnitop-Sanasar road (Rs 15.23 Cr), construction of the DIET building at Asher, Banihal (Rs 11.42 Cr) and the Galli to Kateri road (Rs 7.95 Cr). Covering roads, education, skill development, tribal affairs, social welfare and urban infrastructure, these projects are aimed at improving connectivity in remote areas, strengthening public infrastructure, expanding access to essential services and promoting inclusive development across the district. The meeting was attended by Ministers Ali Mohammad Sagar, Sakina Itoo, Javed Rana, Mir Saifullah, Shamim Firdous and Altaf Ahmed Kaloo; Advisor to the Chief Minister Nasir Aslam Wani; MLA Ramban Arjun Singh Raju; and MLA Banihal Sajjad Shaheen, Additional Chief Secretary to the CM Dheeraj Gupta, heads of departments, district and sectoral officers and other concerned. Deputy Commissioner Ramban Mohammad Alyas Khan made a detailed presentation on the district’s developmental progress, covering highway infrastructure, flood restoration and disaster management, rural development, water and power supply, agriculture and allied activities, education, health, social welfare and urban development. Reviewing the functioning of various departments, the Chief Minister stressed timely completion of ongoing projects, effective inter-departmental coordination and optimal utilisation of available resources. He called for strengthening monitoring mechanisms to ensure that developmental targets are achieved within stipulated timelines. Appreciating the performance of Aspirational Block Khari, which has recently secured a Gold Medal for its achievements in improving developmental indicators, the Chief Minister called for replicating its successful initiatives and best practices across other blocks of the district. He said the experience of Khari should serve as a model for addressing developmental gaps and bringing other blocks to a comparable level of performance. CM Omar also reviewed agriculture and allied sectors, stressing the need to harness the district’s potential. Discussing tourism prospects, he highlighted the potential of destinations such as Kog-Paristan and Nailtop, besides Sangaldan, particularly its hot springs, which could be developed as a health and wellness tourism destination. He called for a focused plan to develop these locations, improve tourist amenities and create better facilities for visitors. Reviewing the education sector, the Chief Minister expressed concern over the need to improve student enrolment in schools and higher education institutions across the district. He directed the concerned departments to identify gaps and take concerted measures to increase enrolment and expand access to educational opportunities. Emphasising the importance of education and skill development, he observed that the aspirations and potential of young people must remain central to the priorities of a responsive government. On healthcare, the Chief Minister stressed the need to expand access to medical facilities, particularly in view of Ramban’s challenging terrain and vulnerability to road accidents. He appreciated the district’s innovative ‘Hospital on Wheels’ initiative, under which doctors, paramedical staff and diagnostic facilities are taken to remote and far-flung areas. He commended the initiative as an effective response to geographical challenges and called for strengthening such efforts to ensure timely healthcare for people in inaccessible areas. The Chief Minister also appreciated the district administration’s focused efforts to reduce road accident fatalities and the overall incidence of accidents along the National Highway. He called for systematic identification of vulnerable locations and accident black spots, followed by preventive interventions to reduce risk of accidents . He stressed that road safety must remain a priority, with coordinated efforts by all concerned agencies to minimise accidents and save precious lives. Reviewing the power sector, CM Omar directed that works under the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) be implemented with equal focus in plain areas and difficult hilly terrains. He stressed that improvements in electricity infrastructure must translate into better quality and reliability of power supply across the district. The Chief Minister also reviewed flood restoration, disaster restoration and mitigation works and directed the concerned departments to expedite their execution. Taking stock of winter preparedness, he called for special arrangements for vulnerable sections, particularly critically ill patients and expectant mothers, directing the administration to ensure their timely shifting to safer locations wherever required. Taking note of progress in digitisation of the revenue sector, the Chief Minister called for further improvements in revenue-related services. He also took up the issue of gypsum mining and directed the concerned Ministers to examine the matter and facilitate necessary clearances in accordance with applicable rules and procedures. Observing that improved road and rail connectivity had opened up new opportunities for economic activity and tourism, the Chief Minister called for leveraging these developments through focused plans for promoting tourist destinations and areas with untapped potential. Taking note of the progress on the Sawalkot Hydroelectric Project, the Chief Minister observed that its execution would generate significant employment opportunities. He directed the district administration to map the skills and trades required for the project and coordinate with the concerned agencies to impart relevant training to local youth under Mission YUVA, enabling them to take advantage of the emerging employment opportunities. The Chief Minister further directed the administration to enhance capital expenditure and ensure that both substantial physical and financial progress is registered before the close of the current financial year. He also stressed timely and complete utilisation of funds available under the Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) scheme, ensuring that allocated resources translate into tangible developmental outcomes. Appreciating the district administration’s efforts in mobilising Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) support for developmental and welfare initiatives, he called for continued efforts to leverage such partnerships to address local needs and strengthen public infrastructure. During the meeting, MLA Ramban Arjun Singh Raju and MLA Banihal Sajjad Shaheen highlighted various developmental demands and issues concerning their respective constituencies, including matters related to tribal welfare, tourism, revenue services and infrastructure development. The Chief Minister took note of the issues raised and directed the concerned departments to examine them for appropriate action. Later, the Chief Minister also interacted with several public delegations, who apprised him of various local issues and developmental demands. He gave them a patient hearing and assured them that their genuine concerns would be examined and addressed on priority.
